name: royal banner pole, 3/4 top-down: square stone foot (top face seen from above, front face), wooden pole with iron bands, gold spear-tip finial, crossbar with a hanging blue banner (gold border, gold crown over a gold eight-point star, swallowtail)
label: beodeul_city/capital/capital_banner_pole

answer.evidence: The only built volume is the square stone foot (rows 56-62, about 10 px wide). Its lighter top face is rows 56-58 (the column scan shows near-white L=219 at rows 57-58). A lightness change at row 59 gives the front-edge line. Below it is a mid-gray front face (rows 59-61, L=176) with a dark bottom outline at row 62. This is a short but real top surface, about 3 rows, with a front face of 3 or more rows. The pole, crossbar, finial and banner are thin vertical elements. The banner and finial are listed as decor, like a flag on a pole. The crossbar is only a 2-row front-facing strip, so I did not count it as a major part missing a top. Facing is south.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse prop, so the per-tile fact is not held against it. Judged by eye, it still looks flatter than the references. The stone foot is a pale block with only 2-3 steps and little grain or per-stone shading. The pole is a thin 1-2 tone line, and the iron bands barely register. The banner is mostly flat blue with a gold border and a small crown and star emblem. It has no cloth folds, no mid or dark ramp, and no swallowtail shading, so it reads as a sticker. Outlines are dark and tinted (0% neutral), but they are used almost uniformly around the shapes instead of being selective, so I call them mixed. Beodeul references such as the well, stall and hedge carry 5-6 steps per material with clustered texture dots, and the candidate is clearly thinner and flatter next to them. Verdict: fail.

styleAnswer.evidence: The prop is thin and sparse, so I judged density by eye rather than by the per-tile count. The outline is tinted, with 0% neutral dark edge pixels, which matches Beodeul's dark-material-tone approach. The shading is shallow, though. The blue banner shows about 2-3 blue steps plus gold trim, and the pole reads as a thin 2-3 tone line with little grain or iron-band modelling. The stone foot is a small, nearly flat pale block with no stone-by-stone shading. Banner, crown and star are legible, and the piece is comparable to the lamp-crook reference. Next to the richer references (stall, well, hedge) it looks flatter and smaller in information, so it falls short of the standard. With the foot and pole this flat, I fail it on the doubt rule.
